projects.title: Hotel Pennsylvania Deconstruction
projects.facility: Former hotel above active rail infrastructure
projects.summary: Moving demolition debris through a vast Midtown hotel while preserving basements and protecting railway infrastructure.
projects.overview:
Hotel Pennsylvania's size and location made debris handling as important as the demolition itself. The former hotel exceeded 1.4 million square feet and 2,000 rooms, opposite Penn Station and Madison Square Garden. NorthStar's contract for Turner Construction combined removal with preservation of three basement levels and protection of active Long Island Rail Road infrastructure beneath the property.

Most demolition used hand methods supported by mini-excavators, demolition robots and skid-steer loaders. A hoist operated within the building footprint, and drive-through openings allowed trucks to load inside. Two steel chutes moved debris across the large floor plates, while high-ceiling ballrooms required engineered shoring during dismantling. Asbestos abatement and environmental remediation were integrated into the work.

Dedicated safety personnel managed entrances and exits in the busy pedestrian and vehicle environment. With handling routes, shoring and access controls built into the sequence, NorthStar reports completing the removal ahead of schedule without incident.

projects.title: Greystone Psychiatric Hospital Demolition
projects.summary: Sequencing abatement and campus demolition while preserving selected historic architectural details.
projects.overview:
The former Greystone Psychiatric Hospital presented two linked tasks: remove deteriorated, asbestos-containing structures and recover selected architectural features for planned reuse. NorthStar's contract for the State of New Jersey combined abatement, demolition and soil remediation across 26 buildings on the former campus.

A 70-person abatement team cleared designated areas before mechanical demolition advanced. Equipment included up to 11 excavators, supported by 150-foot and 125-foot long-reach machines and attachments for concrete, steel and debris handling. Crews salvaged columns and capitals for potential use in a planned memorial.

As structures came down, grid-based tracking identified soil-remediation areas for excavation and approved off-site disposal. NorthStar reports completing the project on schedule despite unforeseen conditions. The work covered former buildings following the opening of the replacement hospital.

projects.title: CCR Impoundment Repurposing — Indiana
projects.period: Started October 2016; completion date not stated
projects.facility: Coal ash impoundment converted for stormwater management
projects.summary: Turning a former coal ash impoundment into a planned three-cell stormwater system.
projects.overview:
An existing coal combustion residuals impoundment in Indiana was designated for a new purpose: stormwater collection and retention. NorthStar's contract required removal of the residuals and reshaping of the basin while drainage was managed through construction. The public profile keeps the client unnamed and records an October 2016 start.

The scope included dewatering, excavation of 600,000 cubic yards of CCR and subgrade, and placement of removed material in an on-site landfill. Borrow-source development, backfill and compaction would establish the new basin geometry. Separation berms, liners and riprap were specified for three cells, with a reconstructed ditch feeding the settling basin.

Pump-structure work, chemical-feed pads, temporary drainage, access-road improvements and final seeding and mulching completed the contracted package. The profile describes the planned conversion and its quantities; a final completion date and operating outcome are not stated.

projects.title: EAA A-1 Flow Equalization Basin
projects.period: Design from July 2013; basin opened August 2015
projects.overview:
The South Florida Water Management District needed a basin that could hold peak stormwater flows and release water steadily to downstream treatment areas. NorthStar provided design engineering for the 15,000-acre EAA A-1 Flow Equalization Basin, taking the project from concept through final construction documents and supporting the work during construction.

The design combined hydrologic and hydraulic modeling, geotechnical investigation, surveying, and civil, structural and electrical engineering. Its principal elements included 13 miles of perimeter levees, 6.7 miles of flow-conveyance levees, water-control structures, canals and remotely monitored gates. The basin was designed to store 60,000 acre-feet of water at an average depth of four feet. NorthStar also reviewed submittals, responded to construction questions and supported as-built documentation as engineer of record.

NorthStar's project profile reports $2 million in identified design optimizations and a construction-cost estimate within 7% of the eventual $60 million construction bid. SFWMD records construction completion in July 2015 and initial water inflow in August 2015. The resulting basin became part of the district's system for managing the timing and treatment of water moving toward the Everglades.

executive.response: NorthStar integrated hydraulic modeling, geotechnical investigation and multidisciplinary design, then provided engineering support during construction.
executive.result: The design provided 60,000 acre-feet of storage. NorthStar identified $2 million in design optimizations; SFWMD records the basin opening to water in August 2015.

projects.title: Kissimmee River Restoration — C-38 Reach 3
projects.overview:
Restoring flow to the Kissimmee River's historic channels required filling part of the straightened C-38 canal and lowering the Bass embankment within the floodplain. NorthStar worked as the primary subcontractor to BCPeabody Construction Services on this U.S. Army Corps of Engineers project, combining large-scale earthmoving with access, erosion and water-quality controls.

The documented scope included approximately 7,000 linear feet of canal backfill using 2.1 million cubic yards of material from adjacent stockpiles, together with lowering approximately 18,500 linear feet of the Bass embankment. Crews cleared stockpile areas, managed turbidity and revegetated disturbed ground. When abandoned pump stations and fuel tanks were encountered, NorthStar coordinated their removal with the Corps and SFWMD.

NorthStar used intermediate earthen plugs to direct water into historic oxbows and limit suspended sediment within work areas. A temporary floating bridge made an otherwise inaccessible stockpile reachable by loaded construction vehicles while maintaining water passage. The project profile records production above 15,000 cubic yards of soil per day, illustrating how access planning and water management supported the earthwork program.

executive.challenge: Backfill a channelized river reach and lower a floodplain embankment while maintaining access and managing sediment in a wet environment.
executive.response: As BCPeabody's primary subcontractor, NorthStar moved stockpiled soil into the canal, installed staged plugs, monitored turbidity and built a temporary floating bridge for equipment access.
executive.result: The documented work placed approximately 2.1 million cubic yards of backfill and addressed 18,500 linear feet of embankment, contributing one defined construction package to the wider Kissimmee restoration.

projects.outcome: 2.1 million cubic yards of backfill supported restoration of historic river flow

projects.title: Four Corners Power Plant — Unit 2 Boiler
projects.overview:
NorthStar's parent-company portfolio includes a short project video of the Unit 2 boiler falling at the APS Four Corners Power Plant in Fruitland, New Mexico. The project entry identifies the specific boiler and facility, preserving a visual record of this part of the plant's decommissioning work.

APS's owner announcement places the work in a broader transition: Units 1, 2 and 3 were permanently shut down in December 2013, with dismantling of those units and associated structures planned to follow. This case entry is limited to the Unit 2 boiler event documented by NorthStar. The public project page does not establish a contract value, NorthStar's full plant-wide scope, the event date or a quantified safety result.

projects.title: Mohave Generating Station
projects.overview:
Southern California Edison contracted NorthStar to decommission the 1,580-megawatt Mohave Generating Station beside the Colorado River. The assignment combined major generating-equipment removal with hazardous-material management, pond closure, landfill work and recovery of assets that still held resale value.

NorthStar's scope covered asbestos abatement, management of oils and other regulated wastes, and demolition of boilers, turbines, large storage tanks and a 500-foot concrete stack. Work initially continued around an active control room, requiring daily coordination over services that had to remain available. Pond closure involved relocating approximately 2.5 million cubic yards of material to the on-site landfill, followed by grading, drainage and closure work.

NorthStar reports recycling more than 40,000 tons of ferrous metal and marketing reusable equipment through an asset inventory, online sales and on-site auctions. The commercial arrangement included a credit to the owner and revenue sharing above an agreed threshold. The published case records more than 300,000 work hours without a lost-time incident and completion to the agreed schedule.

executive.response: NorthStar coordinated abatement, major-structure demolition, earthwork, asset sales and metal recycling within a single decommissioning program.
executive.result: The project profile reports over 40,000 tons of ferrous metal recycled, more than 300,000 hours without a lost-time incident and delivery to the agreed schedule.

projects.title: Washington State University — Martin Stadium
projects.overview:
The first phase of Washington State University's stadium renovation required substantial structural demolition while retaining portions of the existing structure. At Martin Stadium, NorthStar dismantled the press box without removing the foundational podium beneath it, making precision and coordination central to the work.

NorthStar developed the engineered approach with Grid Engineering. Crews coordinated critical crane lifts with equipment-assisted steel cutting so sections could be detached and lowered in a controlled sequence. At ground level, designated staging areas allowed teams to sort, process and load materials for recycling while elevated deconstruction continued.

Working two shifts per day, NorthStar completed its work in eight weeks. The published project account reports no safety incidents and includes feedback from Hoffman Construction recognizing the site's leadership and coordination among trades. The result was a retained podium and cleared structural areas ready for the next renovation work.

projects.title: Moffett Federal Airfield — Hangar One
projects.overview:
At Moffett Federal Airfield, NorthStar worked for AMEC on the abatement and selective demolition stage of Hangar One's revitalization. The former Navy airship hangar required removal of interior buildings, hazardous materials, roofing and siding while preserving the immense steel framework for a later phase of reuse.

NorthStar's phased process combined asbestos and lead abatement with removal of lights, mercury switches and other hazardous components. Crews also collected residual PCB-containing dust before dismantling the buildings inside the hangar. Materials were consolidated or separated at the source to support disposal, salvage and recycling.

The exterior-removal plan covered approximately 850,000 square feet of siding and roofing. A combination of suspended and floor-supported scaffolding provided access, while a balanced sequence advanced along both sides of the hangar to limit uneven loading. The work was designed to leave the steel skeleton, concrete decking and major doors in place for the next stage of rehabilitation.

executive.challenge: Remove contaminated exterior materials and interior buildings from a vast historic hangar without compromising the steel framework intended for reuse.
executive.response: NorthStar sequenced abatement, interior demolition and balanced exterior removal using a combined suspended and floor-supported scaffold system.
executive.result: The documented scope prepared the retained hangar structure for subsequent rehabilitation, with approximately 850,000 square feet of siding and roofing addressed in the removal plan.

projects.outcome: Selective removal preserved Hangar One's steel framework for future reuse
projects.summary: NorthStar's Hangar One scope integrated hazardous-material abatement, interior-building demolition and balanced removal of exterior cladding while retaining the historic structural frame.

projects.title: Hudson River Mill
projects.overview:
NorthStar's work at the former International Paper mill in Corinth covered approximately 50 structures, from large oil tanks and silos to buildings dating to the nineteenth century. The steep site descended roughly 150 feet toward the Hudson River and shared property with two operating power plants and a wastewater treatment facility.

The team had to remove obsolete mill structures while preserving access roads and avoiding disruption to those adjoining operations. The documented scope included more than 400,000 square feet of asbestos-containing roofing, PCB-containing transformers and other regulated wastes, structural demolition and soil remediation. Specialist crews worked concurrently, with as many as 55 people on site.

Material recovery was a substantial part of the program. NorthStar processed more than 70,000 tons of concrete for on-site backfill and recycled more than 16,000 tons of steel and 700,000 pounds of nonferrous material. The parent-company profile records completion on time and within budget.

executive.challenge: Decommission an aging paper-mill complex on steep terrain while protecting roads and services supporting three adjoining operating facilities.
executive.response: NorthStar coordinated specialist abatement, demolition, remediation and asset-recovery crews, processing concrete for reuse and separating metals for recycling.
executive.result: The profile records on-time, on-budget completion, with over 70,000 tons of concrete processed for backfill and more than 16,000 tons of steel recycled.

projects.title: 909 Walnut — Historic Art Deco High-Rise
projects.overview:
The conversion of Kansas City's 35-story building at 909 Walnut into apartments and condominiums required extensive interior removal while preserving historically significant materials for reuse. NorthStar, formerly NCM, was contracted to strip interior systems and finishes and address asbestos, deteriorating lead-based paint and other regulated components.

The assignment had a five-month delivery window and required close coordination with other contractors. At peak staffing, approximately 60 NorthStar workers operated in multiple shifts. The abatement scope included about one and a half miles of piping and 275,000 square feet of vinyl-asbestos tile and mastic, along with thermal insulation and other affected materials. More than 3,000 PCB-containing lamp ballasts and mercury-bearing fixtures were also removed.

NorthStar's source profile records that third-party asbestos and lead clearance sampling passed on the first round. Interior demolition then cleared major areas of carpeting, ceilings, partitions and building systems, preparing the historic tower for its residential conversion.

executive.challenge: Prepare a historic 35-story tower for residential reuse within a tight schedule while protecting significant materials and removing hazardous components.
executive.response: NorthStar combined phased asbestos and lead abatement, regulated-waste removal and extensive interior demolition, with multiple shifts and close contractor coordination.
executive.result: Third-party asbestos and lead clearance sampling passed on the first round, and the interior-removal scope prepared the building for conversion.

projects.summary: NorthStar stripped and abated the historic 909 Walnut tower for adaptive reuse, working around preservation requirements and a five-month delivery window.

projects.title: GSA Federal Office Building 3
projects.overview:
Federal Office Building 3 had housed U.S. Census Bureau employees before a replacement headquarters was built at the Suitland Federal Center. Working within the redevelopment led by Skanska for GSA, NorthStar, formerly NCM, undertook asbestos abatement, interior and structural demolition, material processing and restoration of approximately ten acres.

The site required coordinated work through several building wings, with abatement creating separation for demolition and backfill crews to follow. NorthStar installed stormwater and dust controls, responded to unexpected sinkholes, and used field testing to verify compacted backfill. An on-site project manager and supervisory team coordinated decisions and a recovery schedule after an early delay.

A waste-diversion plan tracked separated materials and weights for the project's sustainability documentation. Approximately 90,000 tons of concrete were processed, with suitable crushed material reused for backfill. NorthStar reports an overall recycling rate above 97% and completion of the recovery schedule, followed by grading, compaction and seeding of the site.

executive.challenge: Remove an obsolete federal headquarters beside the replacement campus while managing asbestos, dust, stormwater and an initially delayed schedule.
executive.response: NorthStar sequenced abatement and demolition by wing, processed concrete for reuse, addressed unstable ground and maintained on-site management and material tracking.
executive.result: The profile reports over 97% recycling, approximately 90,000 tons of concrete processed and successful delivery of the recovery schedule.

projects.outcome: More than 97% recycling supported the removal of an obsolete federal headquarters
projects.summary: NorthStar combined asbestos abatement, building removal, concrete reuse and site restoration at the former Census Bureau headquarters, using phased work and a recovery schedule to coordinate delivery.

projects.title: Edith Green–Wendell Wyatt Federal Building
projects.overview:
The modernization of Portland's Edith Green–Wendell Wyatt Federal Building began with extensive interior demolition and hazardous-material removal. NorthStar worked with Howard S. Wright Constructors on the 18-story federal high-rise, preparing the existing structure for a major sustainability-focused renovation.

Early planning formed an important part of the assignment. NorthStar joined the contractor and other first-tier subcontractors in a team that temporarily worked together inside the building for seven months. This allowed demolition and abatement drawings, specifications, schedules and resources to be coordinated with the other construction packages before and during delivery.

NorthStar's field scope included asbestos and lead-based paint removal; stripping walls, floors, ceilings and mechanical systems; selective structural demolition; and removal of facade and window assemblies. Crews also removed selected elevators, stairways and exterior site elements. This enabling work prepared the building for the subsequent renovation rather than constituting the whole modernization program.

executive.challenge: Prepare an existing federal high-rise for major modernization while integrating demolition and abatement with the needs of multiple construction trades.
executive.response: NorthStar participated in seven months of co-located planning with the delivery team and carried out hazardous-material removal, interior stripping and selective structural and facade work.
executive.result: The demolition and abatement package cleared existing systems and affected building elements for the next phases of modernization.

projects.outcome: Coordinated abatement and demolition enabled a federal high-rise modernization
projects.summary: NorthStar joined the integrated project team early, then performed extensive abatement, interior demolition and selective structural removal at Portland's 18-story federal building.

projects.title: Eagle Point Refinery
projects.overview:
NorthStar, formerly NCM, undertook decommissioning work at Sunoco's former Eagle Point refinery in Westville. The project combined conventional demolition with a sales program aimed at recovering value from newer process assets before they were removed as scrap.

The preparation scope included asbestos abatement and management of former process lines and vessels. An independent consultant supported the asbestos survey, sampling, area clearances and removal documentation. NorthStar was responsible for initial line openings and cleaning of former process equipment before demolition could proceed.

Once areas were prepared, mechanical equipment with shears, grapples, hammers and processing attachments dismantled structures and handled material. At peak activity, ten large machines and operators supported this work. NorthStar's asset team used an equipment catalogue and targeted marketing to generate inquiries and additional asset sales alongside the demolition program.

executive.challenge: Dismantle retired refinery process facilities while managing asbestos and process residues and recovering value from reusable equipment.
executive.response: NorthStar coordinated independent asbestos clearance, process-line preparation, mechanical demolition and an organized asset catalogue and sales campaign.
executive.result: The profile records additional asset sales alongside the removal work, with ten large machines supporting peak demolition activity.

projects.title: BASF Paint Manufacturing Plant
projects.overview:
BASF retained NorthStar to remediate and demolish a former paint manufacturing complex along the Delaware River. The property encompassed approximately 600 acres, with a 17-acre plant footprint. The assignment combined removal of asbestos-containing materials, PCB-contaminated transformers and surfaces, and lead hazards with demolition of the manufacturing and support infrastructure.

Crews removed production, warehouse and administrative buildings, tall steam boilers, power units, water towers and a wastewater treatment plant. Closing the river intake and discharge structures required coordination with the authorities identified in the source profile. Below-grade concrete and paving were removed, and clean concrete was crushed and reused to fill pits, basements and other voids. Final grading and topsoil prepared the former plant area for vegetation. NorthStar reports completion on schedule and within budget, with no OSHA-recordable incidents.

executive.challenge: Close a large industrial complex with several hazardous-material streams, tall structures and river-connected utilities.
executive.response: NorthStar combined asbestos, PCB and lead remediation with structural demolition, intake and discharge closure, concrete recycling and site grading.
executive.result: The former plant area was prepared for vegetated green space; NorthStar reports on-time, on-budget delivery with no OSHA-recordable incidents.

This is general technical context for the profile's separate remediation and clean-concrete reuse work, rather than a site-specific regulatory determination. projects.title: Gannon Station Unit 5
projects.facility: Operating power station and hung boiler
projects.overview:
TECO engaged NorthStar to dismantle an approximately 3,000-ton hung boiler at Gannon Generating Station while a nearby turbine remained in operation. Material could not be dropped. Every steel component had to remain supported and be lowered to the ground, and portions of the boiler framework had to remain because they also supported the adjacent turbine building.

The three-phase sequence began with pneumatic winches lowering steam piping and water-wall assemblies without disturbing the principal support frame. A 300-ton crawler crane then lowered tube bundles through the opened boiler cavity for processing and recycling. Subsequent lifts removed coal hoppers above the operating turbine building, followed by the steam drum and upper structure. The lower 100 feet of framework remained in place to preserve its structural role for the turbine building.

sections.heading: Project story
sections.text:
TECO engaged NorthStar to dismantle an approximately 3,000-ton hung boiler at Gannon Generating Station while a nearby turbine remained in operation. Material could not be dropped. Every steel component had to remain supported and be lowered to the ground, and portions of the boiler framework had to remain because they also supported the adjacent turbine building.

The three-phase sequence began with pneumatic winches lowering steam piping and water-wall assemblies without disturbing the principal support frame. A 300-ton crawler crane then lowered tube bundles through the opened boiler cavity for processing and recycling. Subsequent lifts removed coal hoppers above the operating turbine building, followed by the steam drum and upper structure. The lower 100 feet of framework remained in place to preserve its structural role for the turbine building.

projects.title: A. J. Blotcky Reactor Facility
projects.facility: TRIGA research reactor within an operating VA hospital
projects.overview:
NorthStar served as prime contractor for decommissioning the A. J. Blotcky Reactor Facility inside the Omaha VA Medical Center. The work had to remove the former research reactor and associated contamination while the surrounding medical center continued operating as a hospital. The owner's objective was unrestricted release of the licensed areas and termination of NRC License R-57.

The reactor occupied a steel tank approximately 20 feet deep, requiring controlled vertical access to activated components and concrete. NorthStar dismantled and packaged reactor equipment, removed affected materials and auxiliary systems, and restored the remaining spaces. Flowable fill closed pits, trenches and the reactor tank; penetrations were plugged or capped. Final status surveying, NRC inspections and confirmatory surveying supported release of the facility. The NRC terminated the license on July 22, 2016; future storage, laboratory or office uses were owner plans rather than documented completed conversions.

executive.challenge: Decommission a research reactor inside a continuing-care hospital and demonstrate that the licensed areas met release criteria.
executive.response: NorthStar removed activated components and concrete, managed the waste, restored below-floor spaces and supported final radiological verification.
executive.result: The NRC terminated License R-57 in July 2016 for unrestricted release; NorthStar reports no NRC violations or OSHA-recordable injuries.

projects.title: Former Portland Gas Works Site
projects.facility: Former manufactured gas plant and Fore River shoreline
projects.overview:
NorthStar removed more than 2,000 cubic yards of impacted Fore River sediment at a former manufactured gas plant in Portland. The remediation area extended roughly 50 feet beyond the shoreline. Excavation had to take place in the water while equipment worked from the land side, making access and shoreline support central to the construction method.

Crews installed a substantial steel sheet-pile wall with grouted joints along the shoreline. A long-reach excavator then reached across that boundary to remove the affected sediment. The arrangement provided a land-based working position for the specified river work. NorthStar's profile records a three-month construction period from October through December 2015, a $1.9 million contract and no OSHA-recordable incidents.

executive.response: NorthStar installed a grouted sheet-pile wall and used a long-reach excavator to perform the in-water removal from shore.
executive.result: More than 2,000 cubic yards of impacted sediment were removed during the reported October–December 2015 work period.

projects.outcome: A shoreline support system enabled land-based removal of impacted river sediment.

projects.title: Escanaba Former Tie-Treating Facility
projects.facility: Former railroad tie-treatment site on Lake Michigan
projects.overview:
Union Pacific's former tie-treatment property in Escanaba required sediment removal and construction of shoreline barriers before the onset of winter. NorthStar's scope combined removal of 10,525 cubic yards of impacted Lake Michigan sediment with soil-bentonite and steel sheet-pile cutoff walls. The dredging area extended as far as 170 feet offshore.

Crews built riprap finger piers to support mechanical dredging with a hydraulic clamshell bucket and used positioning controls to guide the removal. Sediment was dewatered and stabilized for off-site disposal, while treated water was reused for dust control. Barrier-wall work proceeded concurrently with dredging. Barges, shoreline equipment and a telescoping conveyor placed the layered sediment cap and backfill. The profile reports nearly 21,000 work hours, no OSHA-recordable incidents and demobilization before late-December winter conditions.

executive.challenge: Complete offshore sediment removal, containment walls and capping within a short pre-winter construction window.
executive.response: NorthStar coordinated pier-supported dredging, sediment processing, water treatment and concurrent barrier-wall construction, followed by layered backfill and capping.
executive.result: The reported scope removed 10,525 cubic yards of impacted sediment and installed both cutoff-wall systems before winter demobilization.

projects.outcome: Concurrent dredging and containment work completed a complex shoreline remedy before winter.

research.context: Michigan's Auditor General identifies Union Pacific's former tie-treatment area at the Escanaba Ore Dock as a cleanup involving soil, sediment, containment walls and caps beside Little Bay de Noc. This corroborates the setting and remedy type; the quantities and construction performance reported here come from NorthStar's project profile.

projects.title: Former Kinston Manufactured Gas Plant
projects.facility: Former manufactured gas plant and Neuse River sediment area
projects.overview:
At Duke Energy's former manufactured gas plant in Kinston, NorthStar combined Neuse River sediment removal with treatment of impacted material on land. A cofferdam provided access to approximately 2,400 cubic yards of river sediment. Crews worked from modular barges with an environmental clamshell bucket, dewatered sediment on the barges and transferred it by truck to a mixing area roughly half a mile away.

The treatment operation blended impacted soils and sediments with cement and slag to stabilize the material in place at an average depth of 18–22 feet below grade. The project profile reports treatment of 62,000 cubic yards to specified strength and permeability criteria. After the material met those criteria, crews installed a vegetated evapotranspiration cap. The reported $6 million assignment extended from November 2013 through May 2015 and recorded no OSHA-recordable incidents.

executive.challenge: Connect river-sediment removal with a large land-based stabilization program and final site capping.
executive.response: NorthStar used a cofferdam and barges for dredging, transferred material to the treatment area, mixed soils and sediments with cement and slag, and installed the final cap.
executive.result: The profile reports 62,000 cubic yards treated to the required performance criteria before capping.

projects.outcome: River sediment removal and soil stabilization were integrated into a capped site remedy.

research.context: North Carolina DEQ's waste-management reporting identifies the Kinston Coal Gas Plant in its contaminated-site inventory. This supplies site context rather than evidence of unrestricted closure. The treatment quantities, schedule and safety record in this case study are specifically those reported in NorthStar's construction profile.

projects.title: Pfizer East Side Remediation
projects.facility: Former manufacturing property and Quinnipiac River wetlands
projects.overview:
Pfizer retained NorthStar as prime contractor to design and construct the East Side Remedial Components at its North Haven property. The assignment translated an EPA-approved remedy into coordinated containment, groundwater collection, capping and habitat work beside the Quinnipiac River. Design investigations, bench-scale testing and regulator coordination supported the transition to construction.

The containment system included approximately 5,425 feet of low-permeability wall, tied into underlying clay, with wells and collection trenches conveying water to the existing treatment system. Wick drains and preload material consolidated former lagoon and pile areas before capping. The scope also included stormwater controls, inland wetlands and tidal remediation, using an on-site soil balance to avoid off-site soil disposal. NorthStar reports approximately 100,000 work hours without an OSHA lost-time accident; final planting and a maintenance period formed part of the restoration scope.

executive.challenge: Deliver a coordinated containment and restoration remedy across an industrial property and regulated river wetlands.
executive.response: NorthStar combined design investigations with a cutoff wall, groundwater collection, consolidation and capping, then integrated drainage and ecological restoration.
executive.result: The profile documents construction of the East Side remedial components and approximately 100,000 work hours without an OSHA lost-time accident.

projects.outcome: Design and construction joined groundwater containment with capping and habitat restoration.

highlights.label: Approximate work hours without a lost-time accident

research.context: EPA's case summary places this work within the larger corrective-action program for the former Pharmacia & Upjohn facility, owned by Pfizer. EPA's sitewide agreement and cleanup value cover a broader program than NorthStar's $23.5 million East Side contract; those program totals are not presented as contractor scope or revenue.

projects.title: Camden Manufactured Gas Plant Stabilization
projects.facility: Former gas works property planned for a new substation
projects.overview:
PSEG's former manufactured gas plant in Camden required remediation ahead of a planned substation. NorthStar's scope began with demolition of a gas holder and smaller structures, including associated asbestos and utility work. Crews then excavated nearly 50,000 tons of affected soil for off-site disposal and treated more than 24,000 cubic yards of remaining soil by in-situ stabilization.

Excavator-mounted mixing combined treatment reagents with soil at depths reaching approximately 30 feet. Perimeter sheet piling and careful utility investigation addressed the nearby gas main and public-street infrastructure, while a temporary water-treatment system supported the excavation. Engineered fill and crushed stone prepared the property for subsequent construction, followed by perimeter and sidewalk restoration. The source documents a $10.3 million contract and no OSHA-recordable incidents, but its conflicting schedule fields prevent publication of a reliable project date.

executive.challenge: Remediate former gas works soils ahead of utility redevelopment while protecting nearby gas and street infrastructure.
executive.response: NorthStar combined preliminary demolition, off-site soil disposal, excavator-based stabilization, temporary water treatment and engineered backfill.
executive.result: The documented scope removed nearly 50,000 tons of soil and stabilized more than 24,000 cubic yards, preparing the property for planned redevelopment.

projects.outcome: Excavation and stabilization prepared a former gas works property for utility redevelopment.

research.context: PSEG's regulatory filing describes the Camden Gas Works as a multi-parcel cleanup with different remediation and control milestones. That record supports the broader site history, but it does not resolve which dates in the contractor profile apply to this precise scope. The parent profile's 2013–2014 header conflicts with its 2011 start and planned 2012 substation narrative, so this case remains undated.

projects.title: University at Buffalo Materials Research Center
projects.period: D&D completion reported December 2013; license terminated 2018
projects.facility: Pool-type research reactor and laboratory complex
projects.overview:
NorthStar's project profile records decontamination, decommissioning and demolition of the University at Buffalo's Materials Research Center. The former reactor complex included a three-level containment building and a laboratory wing. Reactor fuel had already left the facility before this scope, so the work focused on remaining activated components, contaminated materials, structures and restoration of the site.

Crews handled higher-dose components under shielding, drained the reactor pool in stages and separated concrete into appropriate waste streams. Wire sawing divided approximately 600 tons of concrete into manageable blocks; remote equipment addressed activated material near the reactor base with mist and filtered ventilation controls. Decontamination, abatement and demolition extended to building systems, foundations and below-grade spaces. The contractor reports D&D completion in December 2013. The university subsequently documented final phases in 2014 and NRC license termination in 2018, updating the older profile's pending-license status.

executive.challenge: Dismantle a high-dose research reactor complex while separating radioactive material and completing below-grade demolition.
executive.response: NorthStar used shielding, staged pool drainage, wire-sawn concrete blocks and remote removal methods before demolishing and restoring the facility footprint.
executive.result: The contractor reports completed D&D and demolition; the university confirms that the NRC terminated the license in 2018.

projects.outcome: Reactor dismantling and demolition advanced the campus site to eventual license termination.

highlights.label: License termination confirmed by the university

research.context: The University at Buffalo's official project history states that final decommissioning phases were completed in 2014 and that the NRC terminated its license in 2018. This later owner account supersedes the pending-license statement in NorthStar's older profile. The contractor's reported December 2013 D&D date and the later regulatory milestone are kept distinct.

projects.title: Pearce Creek Sediment Disposal Facility
projects.overview:
NorthStar and Sealaska were contracted by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to improve the Pearce Creek dredged-material disposal facility. The assignment combined extensive regrading with a liner system, rebuilt containment berms and new drainage infrastructure. Together, these elements addressed how the facility would contain material and manage water during continued use.

The detailed project profile describes approximately 700,000 cubic yards of planned excavation and placement, including 450,000 cubic yards to be screened for liner cover. The specified work included a three-layer liner, gas collection, higher and wider berms, and a new sluice and outfall system. The contractor profile records an October 2015 start; Sealaska's 2016 newsletter confirms that liner construction was underway. The quantities describe the contracted scope rather than verified final totals.

executive.challenge: Reconfigure a large dredged-material containment facility with coordinated earthwork, lining, berm and drainage systems.
executive.response: NorthStar and Sealaska's contracted scope combined regrading and screened cover material with a multilayer liner, gas collection and reconstructed drainage.
executive.result: Coordinated earthwork, liner installation and drainage formed a single containment upgrade. Sealaska's 2016 project report documents the liner construction underway.

projects.outcome: A joint NorthStar–Sealaska scope integrated earthwork, lining and containment improvements.
qualifiers: Earthwork quantities are published scope figures; final quantities and completion date were not confirmed.

research.context: USACE's 2013 account describes groundwater concerns at Pearce Creek and explains the need for facility improvements. Sealaska's 2016 shareholder newsletter identifies its construction partnership and confirms liner installation underway that year, complementing the contractor profile's October 2015 start. These sources do not establish a final completion date or reconciled contract value.

projects.title: University of Illinois Nuclear Reactor Laboratory
projects.facility: Mark II research reactor and nuclear laboratory
projects.overview:
The University of Illinois selected NorthStar to decontaminate and decommission its Mark II reactor and nuclear laboratory after an extended safe-storage period. The assignment covered reactor equipment, activated and contaminated structures, associated systems, waste packaging and final removal of the laboratory footprint to support unrestricted site release.

Shielding and partial pool drainage supported removal of higher-dose reactor components. Cutting Edge Services performed specialized wire-saw cutting, while remote equipment addressed activated concrete with mist and filtered ventilation controls. NorthStar also completed asbestos abatement and demolition of the approximately 3,200-square-foot facility, including foundations, tunnels and vaults. The contractor reports completion in August 2012 and no NRC violations or OSHA-recordable injuries. The NRC terminated License R-115 on January 17, 2013 after review of the final survey and confirmatory evidence.

executive.challenge: Transition a research reactor from safe storage through controlled dismantling, waste removal and regulatory release.
executive.response: NorthStar coordinated component removal, specialist concrete cutting, remote demolition, abatement and site restoration, supported by final radiological surveying.
executive.result: The NRC terminated License R-115 in January 2013 and released the site for unrestricted use.

projects.outcome: Decommissioning and laboratory demolition supported unrestricted release of the reactor site.

highlights.label: NRC violations and OSHA-recordable injuries reported

research.context: The NRC's January 2013 notice independently confirms termination of the University of Illinois license and release for unrestricted use. The notice describes regulatory reviews and decommissioning milestones; those milestones are distinct from the contractor profile's August 2012 overall completion date.

projects.title: University of Arizona Nuclear Reactor Laboratory
projects.overview:
The University of Arizona retained NorthStar to decontaminate and decommission its reactor and Nuclear Reactor Laboratory. The objective was to remove the reactor and ancillary systems and reduce residual radioactivity to levels permitting unrestricted release of the licensed area. Fuel removal preceded this contractor scope and is documented separately in the NRC's history.

NorthStar dismantled reactor equipment and support systems, removed affected components and activated concrete, addressed hazardous materials and restored the work area. Final radiological verification supported the university's submission of its final status survey report in December 2011. NorthStar's profile reports completion in November 2011, with no NRC violations or OSHA-recordable injuries. The NRC subsequently terminated License R-52 on February 28, 2012, completing the separate regulatory release milestone.

executive.challenge: Remove a university research reactor and demonstrate that the former licensed area satisfied unrestricted-use criteria.
executive.response: NorthStar dismantled the reactor and supporting systems, removed affected materials and completed decontamination and restoration for final surveying.
executive.result: The NRC terminated License R-52 in February 2012 and released the facility for unrestricted use.

projects.outcome: Research reactor removal and decontamination supported NRC license termination.

highlights.label: NRC violations and OSHA-recordable injuries reported

research.context: The NRC's March 2012 notice confirms that reactor operation ended in 2010, fuel was removed through a separate Department of Energy action, and License R-52 was terminated in February 2012 following decommissioning review. This distinction keeps earlier fuel disposition outside NorthStar's documented dismantling and decontamination scope.

projects.title: West Bank & Vicinity 72 Levee Improvements
projects.event: Hurricane Katrina recovery and flood-risk reduction
projects.facility: Lake Cataouatche western tie-in clay levee
projects.overview:
The WBV 72 levee assignment formed part of the New Orleans region's post-Katrina hurricane and storm-damage risk-reduction program. The design moved the new levee alignment behind the existing embankment and raised it, rather than simply building directly on the older levee. Weak foundation soils and a fast construction schedule shaped the earthwork sequence.

NorthStar's profile describes construction of approximately 2.4 miles of levee with about 900,000 cubic yards of excavation and placement. Crews used geotextile reinforcement, borrow-pit dewatering and moisture conditioning, with settlement monitoring along the alignment. Existing levee material and access routes were incorporated into the work sequence. NorthStar performed the earthwork and oversaw a subcontractor's two bridges. The profile reports delivery within budget and the required schedule, with no OSHA-recordable incidents.

executive.challenge: Build a taller, offset levee on weak soils while meeting an accelerated regional flood-risk-reduction schedule.
executive.response: WRS Infrastructure & Environment, later acquired by NorthStar, coordinated reinforced earthwork, borrow preparation, dewatering, settlement monitoring and bridge subcontracting along the new alignment.
executive.result: The reported 2.4-mile construction scope was delivered within budget and schedule, adding to the regional risk-reduction system.

projects.outcome: Large-scale earthwork delivered an improved levee alignment for the regional protection system.

research.context: USACE places WBV 72 within the West Bank and Vicinity system and identifies WRS Infrastructure & Environment as the contractor. NorthStar acquired WRS in 2014. The agency's contract register records a March 2010 award and an October 2012 substantial-completion field, which differ from the dates in the contractor profile; a reconciled project period is therefore not stated. Quantities and performance figures shown here remain attributed to NorthStar's published project account.

projects.title: Sanford Manufactured Gas Plant
projects.facility: Former gasification plant and Cloud Branch Creek corridor
projects.overview:
Progress Energy retained NorthStar for a combined soil-remediation and drainage-construction assignment at the former Sanford manufactured gas plant. The scope included demolition of three abandoned structures, excavation of approximately 20,000 cubic yards of shallow unsaturated soils and deep soil mixing of 125,000 cubic yards of saturated soils. Utility relocation and creek improvements had to be coordinated with the treatment work.

Large mixing augers blended cement and slag reagents into the saturated ground in overlapping columns, supported by survey controls, repeated mixing and verification sampling. The civil scope included nearly 1,000 feet of large box culverts, creek realignment and approximately 450 feet of open-channel improvements along Cloud Branch Creek toward Mill Creek. The profile reports a $14 million assignment from July 2009 through September 2010 and no OSHA-recordable incidents. Later monitoring and sitewide controls remained part of the wider cleanup program.

executive.challenge: Treat a large volume of affected ground while relocating utilities and rebuilding drainage through a former gas plant site.
executive.response: NorthStar combined shallow excavation and deep soil mixing with structural demolition, box-culvert installation and channel improvements.
executive.result: The documented scope treated 125,000 cubic yards by deep mixing and completed the associated soil-removal and drainage-construction work.

projects.outcome: Soil treatment and creek infrastructure were delivered as one coordinated remediation scope.

research.context: EPA's Sanford Gasification Plant profile describes a larger Superfund cleanup with subsequent groundwater monitoring, land-use controls and later construction-completion milestones. Its sitewide treatment quantities differ from this contractor's 125,000-cubic-yard deep-mixing scope. This case does not present the construction contract as unrestricted site closure.

projects.title: Kissimmee River Restoration — Contract 13B
projects.facility: Reach 4 river channel, oxbows and C-38 canal
projects.overview:
NorthStar's portfolio records the Kissimmee River Reach 4 work delivered by WRS Infrastructure & Environment, which NorthStar acquired in 2014. Contract 13B combined canal backfilling and oxbow excavation to help reconnect the river's historical flow path. The documented assignment was one construction package within the much larger Kissimmee River restoration program.

The scope included backfilling approximately 19,300 feet of the C-38 canal and mechanically and hydraulically excavating oxbow channels. Temporary roads, culverts, canal plugs and diversion arrangements supported access and water control during the work. Environmental measures included turbidity monitoring and gopher-tortoise relocation. The profile reports a $18.2 million contract with no OSHA-recordable incidents. projects.title: University of Washington Nuclear Reactor
projects.facility: Former university research reactor on an occupied campus
projects.overview:
NorthStar's portfolio documents service as the University of Washington's decommissioning operations contractor for its former nuclear research reactor. The assignment removed hazardous and radioactive material above unrestricted-release limits to support termination of NRC License R-73. Work took place in a campus setting where surrounding student and teaching activities continued, with confined-space conditions adding to the access constraints.

The scope included activated concrete from the reactor shield and pedestal, affected equipment and surfaces, hazardous-material abatement and characterization of a waste-retention tank. Ventilation decontamination also addressed legacy contamination described in the project profile. Materials were segregated and packaged for appropriate disposal, followed by verification of the remaining facility. The parent profile records completion in November 2006. The NRC's 2007 notice independently confirms termination of the correct license, R-73, and release for unrestricted use.

executive.challenge: Remove reactor-related contamination within an occupied campus setting and demonstrate that the licensed space met release requirements.
executive.response: The documented decommissioning scope combined controlled concrete and equipment removal, ventilation decontamination, hazardous-material abatement and waste management.
executive.result: The NRC terminated the University of Washington's License R-73 in August 2007 and released the facility for unrestricted use.

projects.title: Ole Miss Honors College
projects.outcome: A coordinated mitigation and reconstruction program addressed 6,300 square feet across an academic building.

executive.challenge: Winter storm water-line breaks affected approximately 6,300 square feet from the third floor to the basement. Classrooms, offices, study spaces and a timber-ceilinged Great Room required different recovery decisions within one connected building.
executive.response: NorthStar extracted water, placed drying equipment and organized the work into five priority areas. The scope combined moisture assessment, protection of furnishings and books, selective removal and reconstruction. A dedicated drying approach was proposed for the Great Room’s 1,260-square-foot wood ceiling.
executive.result: Separate final invoices document both mitigation and reconstruction, totaling 3,289 billed labor hours and $374,548.58. The record establishes the scale of delivered services; it does not establish a building-wide reopening date or the final disposition of every finish.

sections.heading: Keeping an academic building recoverable
sections.text: The Sally McDonnell Barksdale Honors College brings teaching, individual study and shared academic life together. A water loss in that setting affects more than floor finishes: it disrupts access to classrooms, workspaces and the materials used in them. NorthStar’s initial scope describes two winter storm losses that carried water from the third floor through lower levels to the basement.

sections.heading: Different spaces, different decisions
sections.text:
The response divided the building into five priority areas. Extraction and equipment placement stabilized affected spaces while the team assessed carpets, wall cavities, ceilings and built-in features. Selective removal was planned where damaged material could not be retained, with like-for-like reconstruction following mitigation.

The Great Room presented a distinctive preservation challenge. Rather than assuming its 1,260-square-foot wood ceiling needed replacement, the scope proposed a contained drying arrangement to direct heated, dry air toward it. Elsewhere, work near electrical panels required coordination before access, while furnishings and books needed protection or careful handling.

sections.heading: The scale behind the response
sections.text: The mitigation invoice records 1,568 labor hours and $177,683.60. Reconstruction adds 1,721 hours and $196,864.98. Together, the two phases represent approximately 3,300 billed labor hours and $375,000 in invoiced work. Overlapping billing periods reflect a staged program; they are not added together to create an inflated project duration.

projects.title: Extended Stay America — Fayetteville
projects.facility: Extended Stay America, 4105 Sycamore Dairy Road
projects.outcome: A three-level hotel recovery effort organized 21 priority areas and more than 17,600 billed labor hours.

executive.challenge: Fire, smoke, soot and suppression-related water affected the hotel’s entrance, shared amenities, building services and guestrooms. Restricted access and limitations on electrical power shaped the initial response, while concealed damage required coordination with the owner, engineers and authorities.
executive.response: NorthStar developed a 21-area recovery scope spanning three levels. The plan distinguished heavily damaged spaces requiring removal to framing from rooms needing selective material removal, cleaning and odor treatment. Stabilization, contents handling and access coordination formed the foundation for the recovery effort.
executive.result: A progress invoice and subsequent final invoice document 17,629 billed labor hours and $1,973,260.81 in combined charges. Project photographs show exposed and treated framing. These records substantiate a substantial recovery effort without establishing a hotel reopening date.

sections.heading: An entrance loss with a building-wide scope
sections.text: At the extended-stay property on Sycamore Dairy Road, the documented damage reached beyond the entrance canopy. Breakfast and fitness areas, guest and house laundry, the lobby, service rooms, stairwells, corridors and guestrooms all appeared in the initial recovery plan. The 21 priority areas provided a practical way to organize different damage conditions across three levels.

sections.heading: Access determined the early sequence
sections.text:
The initial record describes fire-marshal access restrictions, a fire watch and limitations on bringing electrical power into the building. Those constraints mattered because drying, detailed assessment and removal could not proceed as if this were an unrestricted site. NorthStar’s scope required coordination with the owner’s team, engineering and other building trades as conditions were evaluated.

The proposed work varied by area: removal to framing in heavily affected shared spaces; selective treatment of water-damaged materials elsewhere; and detailed cleaning, odor treatment and contents decisions. Proposed structural replacement and rebuilding activities are not presented here as independently verified completed work.

sections.heading: A measured operational scale
sections.text: The first invoice records 10,692 labor hours; the second records 6,937. Their weekly labor summaries cover successive periods, yielding 17,629 hours in total. Combined charges are approximately $2.0 million. This is invoiced project value, not a property valuation or an estimate of avoided business interruption.

projects.title: Dave Smith Motors — Roof Recovery
projects.outcome: A property-by-property roof strategy across three Idaho communities, with distinct repair and replacement options.

executive.challenge: Storm-related roof conditions varied across the Dave Smith Motors portfolio. Shingle, metal-panel and membrane systems required different details, while proposed repair boundaries and replacement recommendations had to be reconciled across multiple addresses.
executive.response: NorthStar’s February proposal set out 19 priced property scopes and two alternative program budgets. The scope addressed roof systems, insulation, flashing, fasteners, coping, gutters and ventilation. It also identified locations requiring reinspection before a repair option could be confirmed.
executive.result: The proposal quantified 57,000 square feet of replacement areas, excluding unmeasured roofs and refastening-only work. A later July tracking workbook records 331 direct labor and travel hours. It does not establish that every proposed property scope was completed.

sections.heading: A portfolio problem, not one roof detail
sections.text: Dave Smith Motors operates across Idaho’s Silver Valley and Coeur d’Alene area. The supplied proposal covers three communities and 19 priced property scopes. Some locations called for limited flashing or fastener repairs; others involved replacement of complete roof sections and insulation. Treating those conditions as a single uniform repair would hide the real decisions facing the owner.

sections.heading: Making the alternatives visible
sections.text:
NorthStar distinguished agreed scope items from locations where its replacement recommendation differed from the alternative repair approach. The two overall proposal options were $694,379.45 and $871,198.47. They are alternatives, not amounts to add together.

The proposal also called for reinspection at eight addresses before confirming repair feasibility. Two additional building IDs were specifically identified as having no observed storm-related damage. Mobilization, traffic controls and roof access had to be considered across the property group.

sections.heading: Quantifying what the record supports
sections.text:
Unique quantified replacement areas total 570 roofing squares, or 57,000 square feet. This subtotal excludes repeated installation steps, shingle purchasing waste, a separate 45-square refastening scope and a roof replacement without a stated area.

The July workbook contains 331 tracked direct labor and travel hours, reconstructed from its populated weekly rows. These cover NorthStar’s recorded coordination and support effort; roofing subcontractor crew hours are not separately itemized. Completion of the entire February program cannot be inferred from that later tracking file.

timeline.text: Price agreed repairs alongside NorthStar replacement recommendations.

timeline.text: Track direct labor and specialist work; validate completed scope against the selected program.

qualifiers: This case documents scope development and project coordination. Proposed budgets are alternatives; 57,000 SF is a partial replacement subtotal. Tracked hours exclude unitemized subcontractor labor. The records do not verify completion of all 19 proposed scopes.

projects.title: Land Rover Santa Monica
projects.facility: Parts and service facility, Olympic Boulevard
projects.outcome: Controlled remediation and ceiling reinstatement in the offices and support spaces behind an automotive service operation.

executive.challenge: The initial assessment identified rodent-related contamination above ceilings, around ductwork and in parts-storage and office areas. Access to concealed surfaces had to be coordinated with protection of furnishings, inventory and occupied business functions.
executive.response: NorthStar organized containment, selective removal and detailed cleaning around the affected support areas. The work progressed into replacement of insulation and ceiling components, with protection of furniture and equipment and staged removal of temporary barriers.
executive.result: The June 17 report marks remediation complete and reconstruction 75% complete. Its detailed work log records 1,523 square feet of installed insulation across nine areas. The two phase workbooks contain 1,365.1 tracked labor and travel hours and approximately $238,000 in combined pre-tax tracked charges.

sections.heading: Working above an active business environment
sections.text: The Olympic Boulevard property houses Land Rover Santa Monica’s service operation separately from its sales location. The affected offices and parts areas support that operation. Contamination above suspended ceilings created an access problem: porous insulation, ceiling components, duct surfaces and densely packed services all required separate treatment decisions.

sections.heading: Control, clean, reinstate
sections.text:
The scope called for controlled work areas, protection of furnishings and equipment, selective removal of affected porous materials and detailed cleaning of retained surfaces. The project record then documents a transition into insulation installation, finish-area cleaning and removal of temporary protection.

Nine room-by-room insulation quantities in the June report total 1,523 square feet. This is a documented installed component quantity, not the building’s floor area. The remediation workbook separately identifies an 11,000-square-foot scope.

sections.heading: A staged handoff
sections.text:
The June 17 progress report distinguishes completed remediation from reconstruction still in progress. Later workbook snapshots track approximately $237,544 in combined pre-tax charges across the two phases. Summing the populated weekly labor rows produces 1,365.1 hours, including travel and excluding subcontractor hours not itemized in those rows.

The important operational story is the coordination of concealed-space access, contents protection and reinstatement. The available records do not support a claim of uninterrupted operations or a final building-wide clearance.

projects.title: New York Hilton Midtown
projects.outcome: A targeted drying and selective-removal response across 26 guestrooms connected by a vertical building-system loss.

executive.challenge: A failed component in an A/C riser in guestroom 4229 allowed water to migrate through the building, affecting 26 guestrooms. Double-layer drywall around chases, dispersed room access and the holiday-weekend operating calendar complicated the response.
executive.response: NorthStar completed assessment, moisture mapping and equipment placement in the affected rooms by May 22. The field report lists 25 dehumidifiers and 47 air movers. The strategy was to dry recoverable material in place, then selectively open areas that were not progressing, coordinating with hotel staff responsible for buildback.
executive.result: The final mitigation invoice records 522 labor hours and $118,641.41 including tax for the May 20–June 5 billing period. Project photographs document drying equipment and targeted chase access. The record does not specify when every room returned to inventory.

sections.heading: Following the water through the building
sections.text: The loss began at a riser component in one guestroom but affected a dispersed set of 26 rooms. This was a building-system problem with room-by-room consequences. NorthStar’s team had to locate moisture, gain access and coordinate equipment across guestroom interiors rather than treat the loss as a single open work area.

sections.heading: Preserve material where drying could succeed
sections.text:
The May 22 field report records completed assessment, moisture mapping and equipment placement. Twenty-five dehumidifiers and 47 air movers supported the initial drying effort. The scope prioritized drying in place, with selective removal where readings failed to improve.

Double-layer drywall around the chases increased the importance of verification before closing work areas. Temporary containment and dust-control equipment were specified for removals, with the hotel’s own team following behind to reinstall materials. The holiday weekend added a scheduling constraint to access, monitoring and trade coordination.

sections.heading: A bounded, documented recovery effort
sections.text: The final invoice totals $108,970.30 before tax and $118,641.41 including tax, supported by 522 billed labor hours. These figures cover NorthStar’s mitigation scope. They do not include a documented total for hotel-managed buildback, establish room-reopening dates or quantify avoided revenue loss.

projects.title: Belterra Park — Flood Recovery
projects.outcome: A distributed flood-cleanup operation spanning roughly 227,000 square feet of barns, dormitories and support facilities.

executive.challenge: River flooding affected the racing facility’s barn stalls, employee dormitories, shared support buildings, maintenance spaces and trackside areas. Saturated contents and deposited sediment created a broad cleanup and logistics challenge across a working campus.
executive.response: NorthStar organized five priority areas with a combined scoped floor area of 226,826 square feet. The response coordinated muck-out, debris handling, cleaning, contents decisions and equipment movement. The April 28 report lists 91 personnel and tracks progress separately across the facility.
executive.result: The April 28 report records the barn-stall muck-out milestone and completion of 54 lower-level dorm rooms, while other cleaning areas remained in progress. The initial budget was approximately $1.5 million including stated tax and allowance. Boyd subsequently announced a May 3 start for the 2025 racing season; that announcement does not establish NorthStar’s full completion date.

sections.heading: Five recovery zones across a racing campus
sections.text: The scope described more than 1,000 barn stalls, 54 lower-level employee dorm rooms, shared shower facilities, maintenance space and a range of trackside and support uses. Adding the five distinct floor-area totals yields 226,826 square feet, rounded to approximately 227,000. Surface-cleaning quantities, wall areas and the repeated references to concrete floors are not added a second time.

sections.heading: The logistics of removing sediment
sections.text: The work involved a combination of equipment-assisted muck-out, detailed cleaning and contents handling. The project reports describe sediment stockpiles, coordination with facility equipment for disposal, and cleaning that progressed by barn, room and support area. A 91-person reported workforce illustrates the coordination burden; it is a dated staffing snapshot, not a claim that the same crew size worked every day.

sections.heading: Progress and planning scale
sections.text:
By April 28, the report marked the broad barn-stall muck-out item and the 54 lower-level dorm rooms complete, with additional cleaning and other areas still progressing. The budget totaled $1,504,183.26 including stated tax and a 5% allowance; a final invoice is not included in the supplied record.

For planning comparison only, maintaining 91 people over 10–16 workdays at 8–10 hours a day produces roughly 7,300–14,600 crew-hours. This is a modeled range based on stated assumptions, not actual timecard evidence. The actual total could differ as staffing ramped up or demobilized.

timeline.label: Mobilize
timeline.text: Assess affected facilities and mobilize labor and equipment into priority areas.

timeline.label: Clear & clean
timeline.text: Coordinate muck-out, contents decisions, cleaning and debris movement.

timeline.label: Track by area
timeline.text: Record completion and remaining work separately across barns, dormitories and support spaces.

qualifiers: Planning labor scenario: approximately 7,300–14,600 crew-hours, assuming 91 people × 8–10 hours/day × 10–16 workdays. Actual total hours and final invoiced value are not supplied. The project is dated 2025 from its underlying records.

research.context: Boyd Gaming’s 2025 announcement describes Belterra Park as a combined gaming and thoroughbred-racing destination and announces live racing from May 3. That provides operating context for the April recovery effort; it is not evidence that NorthStar completed every work area by that date.
